system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
Auxiliary aids and alternative accessible formats
diagnosis: Effective communication accommodation for a patient with a vision disability
mechanism: Federal disability-rights requirements call for communication with patients with vision disabilities to be as effective as communication with others. When necessary, covered health programs should provide appropriate auxiliary aids or services such as qualified readers, Braille, large print, or accessible electronic formats, with the choice guided by effective communication and the individual's needs.
vignette: A 63-year-old woman with severe visual impairment is being counseled about a new long-term medication. She independently manages her health decisions but cannot read the standard-print medication instructions. She asks for the information in an electronic format compatible with her screen reader.
lead: Which response by the clinic is most appropriate?
correct: Provide the instructions in an accessible electronic format that permits effective communication
distractors: Require a family member to read the standard-print instructions to her
Provide the standard-print instructions because the same document is given to all patients
Ask her to sign a waiver stating that written instructions cannot be provided
Withhold written information and rely only on a brief verbal summary
distractor_notes: A support person does not remove the covered entity's responsibility to ensure effective communication when an auxiliary aid or accessible format is needed.
Providing identical inaccessible material does not make communication equally effective for a patient with a vision disability.
The appropriate response is to furnish an effective auxiliary aid or accessible format rather than shift the accessibility burden to the patient.
The nature and complexity of the communication matter; an accessible format can provide the same information independently rather than unnecessarily limiting the patient to a shortened summary.
key_expl: HHS disability-rights rules require covered health programs to take appropriate steps to ensure communication with people with vision disabilities is as effective as communication with others. Auxiliary aids and services can include Braille, large print, qualified readers, and accessible electronic information usable with a screen reader.
objective: Apply disability-access principles by selecting an effective accessible format for a patient with visual impairment rather than relying on family members, inaccessible standard print, waivers, or reduced information.

outline: Disorders of sexual development and puberty
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Familial male-limited precocious puberty (testotoxicosis) due to activating LHCGR variants
mechanism: Activating LHCGR variants can constitutively activate the luteinizing hormone/chorionic gonadotropin receptor in Leydig cells even without ligand binding. The resulting gonadotropin-independent testosterone production causes male sexual development in early childhood; inheritance is autosomal dominant with clinical expression limited to males.
vignette: A 4-year-old boy is evaluated for rapid linear growth, deepening of the voice, pubic hair, and progressive penile enlargement. Serum testosterone is elevated, whereas luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are suppressed. His father had similar pubertal changes beginning at age 3. His mother and older sister are unaffected. He has no café-au-lait macules.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this child's findings?
distractor_notes: Central precocious puberty reflects premature hypothalamic GnRH activation and therefore does not fit a ligand-independent, male-limited familial pattern with suppressed gonadotropins.

McCune-Albright syndrome can cause peripheral precocious puberty, but it is a mosaic GNAS disorder typically accompanied by other characteristic findings such as café-au-lait skin pigmentation and fibrous dysplasia; it is not an autosomal-dominant male-limited syndrome.

Classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency produces adrenal androgen excess and can accelerate growth and sexual maturation, but the inheritance and endocrine mechanism do not match the autosomal-dominant male-limited LHCGR phenotype.
Loss-of-function LHCGR variants cause Leydig cell hypoplasia with impaired testosterone production and undervirilization, the opposite direction of this patient's androgen-excess phenotype.
key_expl: Familial male-limited precocious puberty is caused by activating LHCGR variants. The LH/hCG receptor becomes constitutively active, stimulating Leydig-cell testosterone production without normal gonadotropin stimulation. Affected boys usually show pubertal changes between ages 2 and 5, and the disorder is autosomal dominant but clinically male-limited.
objective: Recognize familial male-limited precocious puberty from early gonadotropin-independent virilization plus a male-limited autosomal-dominant pedigree and connect the phenotype to constitutive LHCGR activation.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease due to PLP1 dysfunction
mechanism: PLP1 variants disrupt proteolipid protein 1/DM20 production, folding, trafficking, or availability in oligodendrocyte membranes. Because these proteins are major components of central nervous system myelin, the result is hypomyelination and progressive neurologic dysfunction, usually in males with X-linked inheritance.
vignette: A 10-month-old boy has persistent nystagmus, delayed motor development, hypotonia, and progressive difficulty controlling head and trunk movements. Brain MRI shows diffuse hypomyelination. His maternal uncle had a similar childhood neurologic disorder.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
distractor_notes: Alexander disease is a GFAP-related leukodystrophy characterized by abnormal astroglial Rosenthal fibers rather than the classic X-linked PLP1 hypomyelination pattern.
Krabbe disease is caused by GALC deficiency with toxic galactolipid accumulation and demyelination, not PLP1-related hypomyelination.
Canavan disease results from aspartoacylase deficiency and N-acetylaspartate accumulation rather than an X-linked myelin structural-protein defect.
Metachromatic leukodystrophy is a lysosomal sulfatide-storage disorder rather than the PLP1-associated X-linked hypomyelinating leukodystrophy.
key_expl: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease is an X-linked leukodystrophy caused by PLP1 variants. Proteolipid protein 1 and DM20 are major components of CNS myelin; abnormal production or trafficking leads to hypomyelination, nystagmus, motor delay, and progressive neurologic impairment in affected males.
objective: Recognize Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease from early nystagmus, motor delay, diffuse hypomyelination, and an X-linked family pattern.

outline: Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Renal coloboma syndrome (papillorenal syndrome) due to PAX2 dysfunction
mechanism: PAX2 is a transcription factor required for early development of the kidneys and eyes. Pathogenic PAX2 variants reduce functional protein and can cause incomplete renal development with hypoplastic kidneys together with optic-nerve malformations or coloboma; inheritance is autosomal dominant.
vignette: A 12-year-old boy is evaluated for progressive chronic kidney disease. Renal ultrasonography shows bilaterally small, hypoplastic kidneys without numerous cysts. Ophthalmologic examination shows an optic-nerve malformation with coloboma. His father has chronic kidney disease and a similar optic-disc abnormality.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this combination of findings?
distractors: HNF1B-associated renal cysts and diabetes syndrome
distractor_notes: Alport syndrome is a hereditary basement-membrane disorder characterized by hematuric kidney disease with sensorineural hearing loss and characteristic ocular abnormalities, not hypoplastic kidneys plus optic-nerve coloboma.
Branchiootorenal syndrome combines kidney anomalies with branchial-arch and ear abnormalities; the optic-nerve coloboma pattern instead points to PAX2-related renal coloboma syndrome.

HNF1B-related renal cysts and diabetes syndrome commonly features renal cysts and early-onset diabetes or other developmental abnormalities, not the characteristic kidney-plus-optic-nerve coloboma combination.
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease causes progressive formation of numerous renal cysts and typically enlarged kidneys rather than bilateral renal hypoplasia with optic-nerve coloboma.
key_expl: Renal coloboma syndrome is a PAX2-related developmental disorder involving the kidneys and eyes. Affected patients commonly have small hypoplastic kidneys that can progress to kidney failure and optic-nerve malformations, including coloboma. The disorder is autosomal dominant.
objective: Recognize renal coloboma syndrome from the combination of renal hypoplasia and optic-nerve coloboma and connect the phenotype to PAX2-dependent embryonic kidney and eye development.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Pachyonychia congenita due to keratin-gene variants
mechanism: Pathogenic variants in KRT6A, KRT6B, KRT6C, KRT16, or KRT17 alter keratin proteins and impair formation of strong intermediate-filament networks. Friction-sensitive skin becomes fragile and hyperkeratotic, producing severe painful plantar keratoderma and characteristic hypertrophic nail dystrophy, often with oral leukokeratosis.
vignette: An 11-year-old girl has had severe pain from thick calluses on the soles since shortly after she began walking. Walking long distances often produces plantar blisters. Examination shows markedly thickened, dystrophic fingernails and toenails and thick white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa. Her mother has similar foot and nail findings.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this patient's findings?
distractor_notes: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex causes friction-induced skin fragility and blistering, often from KRT5 or KRT14 defects, but does not characteristically produce the combination of severe plantar keratoderma, hypertrophic nail dystrophy and oral leukokeratosis.

Dyskeratosis congenita can produce nail dystrophy and oral leukoplakia, but it is a telomere-maintenance disorder with reticulate pigmentation and major bone-marrow-failure risk rather than the classic painful plantar keratoderma phenotype.

Darier disease causes greasy or wart-like papules with characteristic nail changes and is related to ATP2A2/SERCA2 dysfunction, not the painful plantar callus and hypertrophic-nail phenotype of pachyonychia congenita.
Nail-patella syndrome causes nail abnormalities together with characteristic patellar, elbow and pelvic skeletal abnormalities; severe painful plantar keratoderma is not its defining pattern.
key_expl: Pachyonychia congenita is an inherited keratin disorder in which defective keratin proteins cannot form strong, stable intermediate-filament networks. Painful plantar keratoderma is nearly universal, usually beginning when children start walking, and hypertrophic nail dystrophy is common; oral leukokeratosis can also occur.
objective: Recognize pachyonychia congenita from childhood-onset painful plantar keratoderma plus hypertrophic nail dystrophy and connect the phenotype to defective keratin intermediate-filament networks.
duplicate_probe_terms: painful plantar keratoderma hypertrophic nail dystrophy
